all.title: Exam never checks that a call credited to another gate's section cannot satisfy a gate; a scoring mutant that unions calls over ALL sections passes the full battery and gives a false PASS
all.claim: Mutant of Experiment._check_coverage: the union of `calls` is built from the openings of every section in the trace (`for o in [o for ops in tr["sections"].values() for o in ops]`) instead of the gate's own section's openings. SECTION_ABSENT still checks the gate's own section. The frozen exam passes this mutant in --mutation-mode on all four interpreters. It also passes the full non-mutation battery on 3.11: violations 155/155, valids 36/36 including V32, residuals 11/11, H1-H3 ok (saved stdout: a09_full_battery_stdout.txt). Why it survives: every exam case with two sections either gives the two gates disjoint targets (A:f, B:g in X60-X65, X70, V19, V30, V32, R01...) or leaves the target uncredited everywhere. So a call credited to B is never available to satisfy A. `_expect` compares the per-section unions read from the record, which the mutant does not touch, and Verdict.coverage only for the gate's own targets. Separating harness: gate A exercises f, gate B exercises g; `cov.run("A", g)` then `cov.run("B", f)`. The original refuses NOT_EXERCISED. The mutant scores PASS {'A': {f: 1}, 'B': {g: 1}} although f never ran in A's section: a false PASS. This is the exact class-B property ('credit to the wrong section') the design exists to prevent, and no case pins it.

all.title: With asyncio.eager_task_factory (3.12+), a child task that opens its own run_async section, per the spec's remedy, refuses NESTED_SECTION for the whole trace
all.claim: An eager task's first step runs synchronously on the creator's stack, with no Handle._run between. When a task is created from inside a run_async section A (for example `await asyncio.gather(*(cov.run_async("B", job) ...))` inside A), the child's own `_open(B)` walks into A's registered anchor. _open then raises NESTED_SECTION and records it, and every declaring gate of the trace refuses NESTED_SECTION. The identical harness under the default task factory scores PASS {A:{f:1}, B:{g:3}}. The failing pattern is exactly the remedy the spec prescribes for gather/TaskGroup children, and the spec says it works 'including a loop that runs inside another section'.

all.title: A signal-handler exception landing inside _close (after the anchor is dropped) or inside _open (after the count is bumped) permanently leaks a _THREADS count past tracer exit into later tracers
all.claim: _close sets `o.frame = None` and pops the anchor before `st[0] -= 1`. _open does `st[0] += 1` before `_Opening(...)` and `self._openings.append(o)`. A SIGALRM/pytest-timeout(signal)/Ctrl-C exception can land between those statements, either at an eval-breaker in _close or _open, or inside the profile hook during their own c_call/call events, which then propagates into them. The count is then never decremented: __exit__ only detaches openings whose frame is still set. The entry survives the tracer's exit (`_THREADS = {tid: [9, 68]}` with `_ACTIVE = 0`) and leaks into every later tracer. In a fresh, signal-free tracer the thread's last close no longer removes the hook: sys.getprofile() is still _hook after the section closed. _THREADS is still non-empty after that tracer's exit as well. Diagnostic p_a04_where.py maps the leaking windows to _close lines after `o.frame = None` and to _open's `_Opening.__init__` and `append`. Exceptions landing just before the anchor pop also leave the section 'end: open' with an OPEN_AT_EXIT note although it raised.

all.title: ProcessPoolExecutor (fork) workers spawned inside a section inherit the section's stack, hook and registries: a job that opens its own section raises NESTED_SECTION in the child, and workers keep the profile hook for life
all.claim: On Linux (fork default on 3.10-3.13), ProcessPoolExecutor forks its workers lazily from submit(), that is, from the submitting thread's stack inside cov.run("A"). Each worker's main thread is a copy of that stack. It has the same thread ident, the profile hook installed, and A's anchor registered in the copied _ANCHORS, with _ACTIVE=1. A job that follows the pool remedy and calls `COV.run("B", g)` fails the copied NESTED walk in the child. GateSpecError '[V5:NESTED_SECTION] section 'B' opened on the stack of an open opening of section 'A' of the same trace' then reaches the parent through future.result(), crashing the harness. The parent's own trace records no problem. Independently, an idle worker's sys.getprofile() is still _hook: the Python-level hook stays installed in every such worker for its lifetime, including after the parent's tracer exits, and taxes every call the worker makes.
all.expected_per_spec: Over-blocking #15: 'Child processes are invisible.' #1: 'Off-stack work never counts ... executors ... Remedy: each job opens its own section, with `cov.run` inside the submitted function'. 'Threads, pool workers, executors ... all start at their own bootstrap frame.'
all.observed: job results in parent: ["GateSpecError [V5:NESTED_SECTION] section 'B' opened on the stack of an open opening of section 'A' of the same tr...", same]; a worker's sys.getprofile() while idle in the pool: '<function _hook ...>'; parent trace problems: [].
all.why_not_a_stated_limit: 'Invisible' promises no credit, not a raised refusal in the job or a permanently hooked worker. The message describes a nesting that exists only in the child's copied stack. The claim that pool workers 'start at their own bootstrap frame' is false for forked process-pool workers.

all.title: An opening whose 'end' is unhashable makes score() and check_metrics() raise TypeError instead of refusing BAD_TRACE
all.claim: _check_trace_shape tests `o["end"] not in _ENDS or type(o["end"]) is not str`. The frozenset membership runs first, so an unhashable end (a list or dict, for example from a trace edited or merged by a script) raises TypeError: unhashable type. score() therefore raises TypeError instead of refusing '[V5:BAD_TRACE]'. check_metrics() also raises, because it catches only GateSpecError, although the spec says it 'reports usable: False ... and never raises'. This is outside the attribution lens but was found while reading the scoring path.
all.expected_per_spec: Score step 3 'BAD_TRACE, in one pass before anything is read. Every type check is exact ... `end` is in the enum'; R1-D3 'Exact-type schema validation in one pass before reading' (CLOSED_P); '`check_metrics` ... reports `usable: False` with the refusal text and never raises'.
all.observed: score: RAISED TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'; check_metrics: RAISED TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'.
all.why_not_a_stated_limit: Forgery is an accepted residual, but a malformed trace is supposed to refuse BAD_TRACE (and check_metrics never raise); a crash with a non-GateSpecError is exactly what R1-D3 claims closed.

all.title: Over-blocking #14 is false on 3.10/3.12/3.13: code run only inside a trace callback via sys.call_tracing is credited, so the same harness scores differently by version
all.claim: A settrace callback, as a debugger has, can evaluate code with sys.call_tracing; pdb's do_debug does this. On 3.10, 3.12 and 3.13, sys.call_tracing re-enables profiling for that call. The styxx hook sees the target's call event and walks out through the trace callback frame into the traced section frame, so the section is credited, although the section's own code never calls f. On 3.11, call_tracing does not re-enable profiling and the same harness refuses NOT_EXERCISED. The impact is low, because the credit is for code that ran on the section's stack. But the disclosed sentence is false, and the verdict is version-dependent against the rule that outcomes are identical on 3.10-3.13.
all.expected_per_spec: Over-blocking #14: 'Functions executed only inside profile or trace callbacks can never be credited. That includes the styxx hook itself.' Exam rules: 'Everything must be identical on 3.10–3.13, except the version-keyed cases'.
all.why_not_a_stated_limit: It contradicts a disclosed sentence rather than falling under one; no version key covers it.

all.title: The per-hit f_back walk makes a declared recursive target quadratic in recursion depth (2.8-3.9 s at depth 8000 vs ~1-3 ms untraced)
all.claim: Every hit walks the whole chain to the root or the cut, so a declared recursive target costs O(depth) per hit and O(depth^2) per top-level call. Measured: x4 depth gives x13-x17 traced time. At depth 8000 the traced time is 2.8 s (3.11), 3.9 s (3.10), 3.5 s (3.12) and 3.6 s (3.13), against 1.1-2.8 ms untraced, a 2600x slowdown. The spec quotes the walk cost only 'per hit at depth 30'. A deep recursive-descent target under setrecursionlimit can look like a hang.
all.expected_per_spec: Cost table: 'f_back walk, per hit at depth 30 | about 3–5 µs (100k hits: 0.33–0.46 s ...)'; Over-blocking #17 'Cost ... the per-hit f_back walk'.
all.observed: traced time x16.0 for x4 depth (3.11); depth 8000: 2.8 s traced vs 1.1 ms untraced.
all.why_not_a_stated_limit: The cost is disclosed as a per-hit figure at depth 30; the depth dependence (quadratic for recursion) is not stated. It is reported as a NOTE.

all.title: A stub installed by pre-trace __code__ assignment passes FOREIGN_DEFINITION and is credited as the declared function
all.claim: The provenance check (FOREIGN_DEFINITION) tests only the function object's __globals__. __code__ is writable. Before the trace, a harness can stub a function in place with `real.__code__ = stub.__code__`, where the stub comes from a test module. This is the usual way to stub a function so that captured aliases (`from m import f`, as run_p1 does) also see the stub. The function object is still the real one, so resolution accepts it. Minting then copies the stub's code, and every call of the stub is credited as the declared target, while the real body never runs. The trace even records the stub's file:line under `targets` and never checks it. A second shape also passes: a stub built as `types.FunctionType(stub.__code__, vars(mod))` and bound at the name. This is the J1-X1 class ('stub bound before the trace'), which the closure table lists as CLOSED_P.
all.expected_per_spec: Target identity step 5: 'This closes judge 1's X1: a stub or `monkeypatch` lambda from a test module bound before the trace'. Stated limits, L-STUB: 'Provenance proves where the code was defined, not that it is the original binding. A stub defined in the declared module, or a wraps-stamped stub bound before the trace, is credited (R05, R06).' Finding closure: 'J1-X1 / all designs: stub bound before the trace | CLOSED_P | FOREIGN_DEFINITION by `__globals__` (X26-X30). An in-module stub or a wraps-stamped stub is L-STUB (R05, R06)'.
all.observed: score: PASS coverage={'G': {'rt4_power:reachable': 3}}. The stub returned True three times and the real body never ran. trace targets = {'rt4_power:reachable': '/tmp/.../rt4_teststubs.py:2'}. Variant b (FunctionType(stub_code, vars(mod)) bound at the name) also PASSES.
all.why_not_a_stated_limit: L-STUB names two residuals only: a stub defined in the declared module, and a wraps-stamped stub. This stub is defined in another module and carries no wraps stamp. L-STUB's premise, 'Provenance proves where the code was defined', is false: __globals__ proves where the function object was created, and its code can come from anywhere. CODE_SWAPPED looks only at swaps made during the trace. So this is both an uncovered false PASS and a false sentence in the limit.

all.title: The cache-wrapper 'body' is read from the writable __wrapped__, not from the function the C wrapper calls: false PASS and false refusal
all.claim: For a C lru_cache/cache wrapper, _resolve_target takes F_T = obj.__dict__['__wrapped__']. That is metadata: `functools.wraps`/`update_wrapper` overwrite it. The C wrapper actually calls its internal func, which gc.get_referents shows. Consider `@functools.wraps(Ref.power) @functools.lru_cache def power(n): <fast closed form>`, where Ref.power is a staticmethod reference implementation in the same module. The minted function is then Ref.power, which `power` never calls. (a) A section that calls only Ref.power makes the gate declaring `rt4_cachemod:power` PASS, although `power` never ran. (b) A section that calls only `power` (a cache miss) is refused NOT_EXERCISED. (c) If the reference is a module-level name, the refusal is NOT_A_FUNCTION with the remedy 'declare that name instead'. That remedy names a function the wrapper never calls.
all.expected_per_spec: Resolution step 4: 'Then F_T = body. The target is defined as the cached body: misses count and hits do not.' L-CACHE: 'A cache wrapper's target is its body. Direct calls of the body, through `__wrapped__` or a reference captured before decoration, count (R07).' Step 5 rationale: '`__module__` is a writable string that anyone can set and `wraps` copies.'
all.observed: The cache wrapper's real callee (gc.get_referents) is `power` at line 10, while __wrapped__ claims Ref.power at line 5. (a) Only Ref.power called: PASS coverage={'G': {'rt4_cachemod:power': 1}}. (b) Only power called: REFUSED [V5:NOT_EXERCISED]. (c) Module-level reference: [V5:NOT_A_FUNCTION] '... declare that name instead'.
all.why_not_a_stated_limit: L-CACHE credits calls of the body. Here the minted function is not the body, and it is not reached through the wrapper at all. No limit says that a cache target is whatever __wrapped__ claims, and the spec itself rejects trusting attributes that wraps writes.

all.title: Two distinct cache wrappers of one body share one mint; the uncalled one's gate PASSES
all.claim: Consider two C cache wrappers around the same body, such as an unbounded and a bounded cache made by a helper, where the body is not bound by name. Both declared names resolve to the same F_T and share one mint. A section that calls only `cached_all` credits `cached_small` too. The gate declaring `cached_small` PASSES although `cached_small` was never called: its cache_info shows misses=0, hits=0. This contradicts the design's claim that no two distinct callables ever map to one observed code object. The alias rule was written for two names bound to one object, not for two different wrapper objects.
all.expected_per_spec: 'Because nothing is unwrapped, no two distinct callables ever map to one observed code object; that many-to-one mapping was the root of R2-D2 and R3-D1.' L-CACHE: 'Direct calls of the body, through `__wrapped__` or a reference captured before decoration, count (R07).'
all.observed: sections S: {'calls': {'rt4_twocache:cached_all': 1, 'rt4_twocache:cached_small': 1}}. score PASS for G_SMALL. cached_small.cache_info() = CacheInfo(hits=0, misses=0, maxsize=16, currsize=0).
all.why_not_a_stated_limit: L-CACHE lists direct calls of the body through __wrapped__ or through a reference captured before decoration. A call through a different cache wrapper is neither. The 'no two distinct callables' sentence is false for cache wrappers, because the cache branch unwraps.

all.title: __enter__ failing after minting leaves __code__ minted forever, stops later tracers from restoring, and a retried tracer counts x4 with a spurious CODE_SWAPPED
all.claim: Several exceptions can land between the mint loop and `self._state = 'active'`: `asyncio.events.Handle._run.__code__` raising (Handle._run patched with a MagicMock), an audit hook refusing a `__code__` write, or an asynchronous KeyboardInterrupt or signal timeout. __exit__ never runs, and the minted __code__ stays installed. _MINTED/_BY_FN keep the mint, and m.tracers keeps the dead tracer. After that, (1) a later, completely normal tracer on the same function exits without restoring, because it is never the last holder, so the registries never empty. (2) An innocent outer tracer that was active when an inner tracer's enter failed also exits without restoring its target. (3) Re-entering the same tracer object is allowed, because the state is still 'new'. It appends itself to m.tracers again and duplicates its names in _by_code. One call of f then records f:4, and exit records a spurious CODE_SWAPPED for every target.
all.expected_per_spec: Minting: 'The original code is restored when the last tracer holding the mint exits, and only if fn.__code__ is m.code at that moment.' Exam leftover checks: '_THREADS, _ANCHORS, _MINTED and _BY_FN are empty ... every fixture function's __code__ is its original'. REENTRY: 'If the state is not new, refuse REENTRY.'
all.observed: (i) AttributeError(__code__). Afterwards f and g are still minted, minted=2, by_fn=2. A later normal trace PASSES, but after it exits f_restored=False and minted=2. Retry of the same tracer: calls {'rt4_enter:f': 4, 'rt4_enter:g': 4}, problems [CODE_SWAPPED f, CODE_SWAPPED g], scored REFUSED [V5:CODE_SWAPPED]. (ii) An audit hook refusing g's write leaves f minted. (ii') An innocent outer trace PASSES, but f is not restored after it exits. (iii) A simulated Ctrl-C at the _STOP line leaves f minted.
all.why_not_a_stated_limit: L-ASYNC-EXC covers only the window between _open's registration and run's try. 'Interrupted exit' covers only __exit__. Nothing discloses that a failed __enter__ touches state, or that it blocks restoration for all later tracers and for an enclosing tracer. The x4 count and the CODE_SWAPPED code with nothing swapped are wrong counts and a wrong reason code.

all.title: A tracer that declares asyncio.events:Handle._run leaves _STOP as a dead mint for a surviving tracer; the dispatch cut is lost
all.claim: _STOP is read from `asyncio.events.Handle._run.__code__` after minting at every __enter__, and it is reset only when _ACTIVE reaches 0. If a tracer declares `asyncio.events:Handle._run` (a legal, resolvable stdlib target), _STOP becomes its minted code. When that tracer exits and restores the original while another tracer is still active, _STOP stays the dead mint, and no Handle._run frame ever matches it. The surviving tracer then credits task steps to a section anchored below the loop. The X73 shape, `cov.run('A', asyncio.run, main())` with f called only in gathered child tasks, PASSES. Cross-thread submissions into such a loop (J1-X2) are credited the same way.

all.title: An exception raised inside _hook during _open's `with _LOCK` exit leaves _LOCK held for good, so other threads hang
all.claim: In _open, `sys.setprofile(_hook)` runs inside `with _LOCK:`. So the RLock release is skipped, and the exception leaves _open with _LOCK still acquired. The owning thread never notices because the lock is re-entrant. From then on, every other thread that opens or closes a section, or enters or exits a tracer, blocks for ever. That includes the spec's own remedy for pools, where each job calls cov.run in a worker thread. The traceback of the leaking Timeout is handler <- _hook:724 (or 721) <- _open:1041 (`with _LOCK:`). Probe probe/p15_lock_leak_probe.py recorded 685 leaks in 352k SIGALRM cycles on 3.11. The same window exists at the lock exit of _close and __exit__ whenever the hook is still installed there, for example when an outer tracer's opening is on the same thread. KeyboardInterrupt from Ctrl-C, for instance in a notebook, lands the same way.

all.title: A fork-start child that opens a section hangs for ever on the inherited _LOCK
all.claim: _LOCK is a module-level threading.RLock, and nothing re-initialises it after fork (there is no os.register_at_fork). _LOCK is held by _open, _close, __enter__ and __exit__. The child's first cov.run() then blocks for ever at `with _LOCK:` (protocol.py:1041). Concurrent sections on several threads are the shape the spec blesses (V21, V22, V32), so this is common. fork is the default multiprocessing start method on Linux for every supported version (3.10-3.13). A process-pool job that opens its own section, as the spec advises for pool jobs, therefore hangs, and so does the parent waiting on it. The same happens to a forked child that unwinds through an inherited `run` finally, for example via sys.exit, because _close takes _LOCK.

all.title: The hook's self-removal uninstalls a user's chaining profiler (the foreign profiler is replaced)
all.claim: _hook's self-removal calls sys.setprofile(None) without checking that the installed profiler is its own. A user profiler started inside a section that politely chains to the previous profiler captures styxx's _hook as `prev` and keeps calling it. Once the section closes (tid not in _THREADS), the very next event reaching _hook through the chain removes the *user's* profiler, and it silently stops: 0 events for later calls, during and after the trace. A non-chaining profiler in the same position is left installed. In addition, the close appends PROFILER_LOST, 'calls after that on this thread were not observed', although every call was observed through the chain and the gate PASSes with f:1.

all.title: A RecursionError inside _open leaks a _THREADS entry past tracer exit, and later tracers keep their hook installed after their sections close
all.claim: _open runs sys.setprofile(_hook) and st[0] += 1 before it builds and registers the opening. The next Python frame is _Opening.__init__, whose call event runs the just-installed hook one frame deeper. That is the deepest point of the section, deeper than the hit path when fn itself is the target. A harness that opens a section per level of a recursive walk and catches RecursionError therefore hits the limit exactly at `o = _Opening(...)`. The error comes from _hook on 3.10/3.11 and from __init__'s push on 3.12/3.13. _open raises with the count incremented and no opening to close or detach. The _THREADS entry survives the tracer's exit, so the per-case leftover check would fail. On the next tracer, that thread's count never returns to 0: its hook stays installed after the tracer's last section closes, runs on every later event, and fills uncredited buckets until all tracers exit. No note is written. This is an error path that neither the R2-D4 closure (no handler, the drop is a note) nor the R2-D5 closure (close in run's finally) covers.

Closure R2-D5: "Close runs in `run`'s `finally` (V25 plus the leftover check)". Exam leftover rule: "`_THREADS`, `_ANCHORS`, `_MINTED` and `_BY_FN` are empty and `_ACTIVE == 0`". all.why_not_a_stated_limit: L-ASYNC-EXC covers only an *asynchronous* exception between registration and run's try, and that case leaves a detachable opening. This one is a deterministic synchronous RecursionError *before* registration, leaves nothing to detach, and outlives the tracer. 'Hook loss' covers dropped calls, not leaked registry state.

all.title: After gc.freeze() a live same-globals clone of M_T escapes CLONE_ALIVE and the gate scores PASS
all.claim: CLONE_ALIVE relies on gc.get_referrers(M_T), which scans only generations 0-2 and not the permanent generation. The harness builds FunctionType(f.__code__, f.__globals__), calls it in the section, and keeps it alive past exit. If gc.freeze() has run after the clone was made (a routine pre-fork memory optimisation), the refcount gate opens but the scan finds nothing. No problem is recorded, and the gate PASSes with {'ca_f5:f': 1} although f itself never ran. Without gc.freeze() the same harness is refused CLONE_ALIVE. all.claim: For every step after the module, _resolve_target first calls isinstance(obj, types.ModuleType), then isinstance(obj, type), then isinstance(obj, (staticmethod, classmethod)). When the type check fails, isinstance falls back to obj.__class__ through the object's own __getattribute__. all.title: A failed __code__ assignment mid-mint leaves earlier targets minted and registered forever and escapes __enter__ raw
all.claim: __enter__ resolves every target, then mints them one at a time under _LOCK with no rollback. CPython raises the audit event object.__setattr__ for __code__ assignment. If a later target's assignment fails (for example, a sandbox audit hook that protects vendored code objects), a raw PermissionError escapes __enter__ and the earlier targets stay minted. Their fn.__code__ is never restored. _MINTED and _BY_FN keep a mint whose tracers tuple holds a tracer that never entered, so even a later ordinary tracer on the same function cannot restore it. With the audit hook inert, the same trace is clean.

all.title: A score-side mutant that counts calls from EVERY section passes the frozen exam, so credit taken from another gate's section scores PASS
all.claim: _check_coverage adds up `calls` over the openings of the gate's own section. The mutant adds them up over every section in the trace (`for o in [op for ops in tr['sections'].values() for op in ops]`), so a gate passes if its targets ran in ANY section. The frozen exam passes this mutant on all four Pythons (155/155, 35/35, 11/11, retro exact, 0 crashes). Why the exam cannot see it: every cross-section case (X60-X70) sends the off-section call to `uncredited` or `ambiguous`, never into another section's `calls`. No valid case has one target that is declared by one gate and also called in a different gate's section. Verdict.coverage projects the union onto the gate's own exercises, which hides the extra counts. Harness: gate A declares f; gate B declares f and g. A's section forgets f and calls only g, while B's section calls both. The original refuses A NOT_EXERCISED. The mutant scores A PASS and the experiment verdict PASS. That is the P1 defect itself, and the credit goes to the wrong section. This is the most severe survivor: it breaks the Attribution rule at score time.

all.title: CLONE_ALIVE weakened to 'scan only when the last tracer releases the mint' survives the exam; the nested inner gate PASSes on a live same-globals copy
all.claim: __exit__ runs the refcount-gated CLONE_ALIVE scan for every mint the exiting tracer held. The mutant runs it only when that tracer was the mint's last holder (`if not m.tracers and sys.getrefcount(...) - expected > 0`), which reads like a plausible 'only scan on release' optimisation. all.claim: __exit__ clears _STOP only when _ACTIVE reaches 0. The mutant clears it on every exit. The frozen exam passes it for two reasons. Each case's own tracer sets _STOP again at __enter__. And no case runs work that depends on the cut after a NESTED tracer has exited. Harness: an outer tracer, plus an inner tracer entered and exited inside it (V15's shape). (ii) Closing a started generator suspended at a bare `yield`, from inside a section, runs no body code but is credited on 3.10, 3.11 and 3.13 and not on 3.12 (f01b). all.title: On 3.10 an open section corrupts the traced program: cell writes from other threads are reverted, and deleted locals stay alive
all.claim: On CPython 3.10, sysmodule.c call_trampoline wraps every Python-level profile callback in PyFrame_FastToLocalsWithError(frame) and then PyFrame_LocalsToFast(frame, 1). The second call writes the frame's f_locals snapshot back into its cells (bpo-30744). _hook is a Python function, so while a section is open every event on that thread does this. The GIL can switch while _hook runs, so a closure (nonlocal) write made by another thread in that window is overwritten with the stale snapshot. The snapshot also keeps deleted locals alive until the frame's next own event, which changes refcount-driven behaviour. 3.11+ only write back when f_locals was materialised, and _hook never reads f_locals, so they are unaffected. Two ordinary harness shapes break only inside a section. (1) f09: a worker thread counts into a nonlocal while the section thread polls: 37k–136k of 300k updates are lost. A worker that sets `done = True` once has the flag reverted in 231–239 of 300 trials, so without the script's deadline the harness spins forever. (2) f09b, single-threaded and deterministic: `f = open(p,'w'); f.write('payload'); del f; read_back(p)` reads '' inside a section and 'payload' outside it. Untraced runs of both are clean. A related symptom: finalizers released by the trampoline run inside the profile callback, so on 3.10 their calls are invisible (probe_wr4.py), whereas L-RUNTIME says they count for the stack they land on.

Versions: 'Executed on 3.10–3.13, with identical batteries apart from cProfile'; '3.9 ... is expected to behave like 3.10' (it has the same trampoline).

all.title: On 3.12+ with eager_task_factory, the spec's recommended per-task run_async sections refuse NESTED_SECTION and poison the whole trace
all.claim: The harness combines the spec's two recommended async shapes: `asyncio.run(cov.run_async('A', main))` (Over-blocking #2) and, inside main, `gather(*(cov.run_async('B', job, i) ...))` (#1's remedy: 'run_async inside the task'). With the default task factory it PASSes on 3.10–3.13. On 3.12 and 3.13 with asyncio.eager_task_factory, each child's first step runs synchronously inside create_task on A's stack, with no Handle._run between the two anchors. _open's NESTED walk therefore meets A's opening, and every child raises NESTED_SECTION. The refusal is recorded, so every declaring gate refuses. The spec mentions eager tasks only as a credit effect ('only a child's first synchronous step counts', X82), and it asserts that a task inside any loop may open its own run_async section.

fresh.title: A stub installed by pre-trace __code__ assignment passes FOREIGN_DEFINITION and is credited as the declared function
fresh.claim: The provenance check (FOREIGN_DEFINITION) tests only the function object's __globals__. __code__ is writable. Before the trace, a harness can stub a function in place with `real.__code__ = stub.__code__`, where the stub comes from a test module. This is the usual way to stub a function so that captured aliases (`from m import f`, as run_p1 does) also see the stub. The function object is still the real one, so resolution accepts it. Minting then copies the stub's code, and every call of the stub is credited as the declared target, while the real body never runs. The trace even records the stub's file:line under `targets` and never checks it. A second shape also passes: a stub built as `types.FunctionType(stub.__code__, vars(mod))` and bound at the name. This is the J1-X1 class ('stub bound before the trace'), which the closure table lists as CLOSED_P.

A stub defined in the declared module, or a wraps-stamped stub bound before the trace, is credited (R05, R06).' fresh.claim: For a C lru_cache/cache wrapper, _resolve_target takes F_T = obj.__dict__['__wrapped__']. That is metadata: `functools.wraps`/`update_wrapper` overwrite it. The C wrapper actually calls its internal func, which gc.get_referents shows. The minted function is then Ref.power, which `power` never calls. (a) A section that calls only Ref.power makes the gate declaring `rt4_cachemod:power` PASS, although `power` never ran. (b) A section that calls only `power` (a cache miss) is refused NOT_EXERCISED. (c) If the reference is a module-level name, the refusal is NOT_A_FUNCTION with the remedy 'declare that name instead'. After that, (1) a later, completely normal tracer on the same function exits without restoring, because it is never the last holder, so the registries never empty. (2) An innocent outer tracer that was active when an inner tracer's enter failed also exits without restoring its target. (3) Re-entering the same tracer object is allowed, because the state is still 'new'. It appends itself to m.tracers again and duplicates its names in _by_code. fresh.title: An exception raised inside _hook during _open's `with _LOCK` exit leaves _LOCK held for good, so other threads hang
fresh.claim: In _open, `sys.setprofile(_hook)` runs inside `with _LOCK:`. When the with block ends it calls the C method `_LOCK.__exit__`, which fires a 'c_call' profile event, so _hook runs at that point. The spec lets an exception raised in the hook propagate "as CPython defines". When a profile function fails on a c_call event, CPython does not make the C call at all. So the RLock release is skipped, and the exception leaves _open with _LOCK still acquired. The owning thread never notices because the lock is re-entrant. From then on, every other thread that opens or closes a section, or enters or exits a tracer, blocks for ever. That includes the spec's own remedy for pools, where each job calls cov.run in a worker thread. The traceback of the leaking Timeout is handler <- _hook:724 (or 721) <- _open:1041 (`with _LOCK:`). Probe probe/p15_lock_leak_probe.py recorded 685 leaks in 352k SIGALRM cycles on 3.11. The same window exists at the lock exit of _close and __exit__ whenever the hook is still installed there, for example when an outer tracer's opening is on the same thread. KeyboardInterrupt from Ctrl-C, for instance in a notebook, lands the same way.

The loss is recorded as a PROFILER_LOST note at close, and afterwards that thread only under-counts." Stated limits: "Re-entry through finalizers or signal handlers. ... the RLock serializes it. The worst case is lost counts plus a spurious note." Finding closure R3-D3: "CLOSED_S | The hook and record() take no lock; one RLock covers the rest".

fresh.title: The hook's self-removal uninstalls a user profiler that chains to it
fresh.claim: _hook's first branch runs sys.setprofile(None) without checking that it is the installed profiler. fresh.title: A declared generator or coroutine whose body never runs is credited (false PASS) on 3.10/3.11; 3.12 differs again on close-at-yield

On 3.10 and 3.11 this happens when an unstarted generator is dropped (its finaliser calls gen_close) and when an unstarted generator or coroutine is explicitly .close()d. f_back is the harness frame, so _hook credits the open section. The result is the P1 defect exactly: the harness calls the generator function and forgets to consume it (`mod.scan(rows)` instead of `list(mod.scan(rows))`), or builds a coroutine and closes it to silence 'never awaited'. The trace records {scan: 1}/{fetch: 1} and score() returns PASS, although BODY_RAN stays empty. On 3.12 and 3.13 the same harness is NOT_EXERCISED, because gen_close skips frames in the CREATED state. Two related shapes: (i) throw() into an unstarted generator or coroutine credits on all four versions (probe_throw.py). (ii) Closing a started generator suspended at a bare `yield`, from inside a section, runs no body code but is credited on 3.10, 3.11 and 3.13 and not on 3.12 (f01b). That is a 3.12-only split, not a <=3.11 vs >=3.12 one, and partial-consumption counts differ the same way ({gen:2} vs {gen:1}). None of this is in the spec's Versions section.

fresh.title: On 3.10 an open section corrupts the traced program: cell writes from other threads are reverted, and deleted locals stay alive
fresh.claim: On CPython 3.10, sysmodule.c call_trampoline wraps every Python-level profile callback in PyFrame_FastToLocalsWithError(frame) and then PyFrame_LocalsToFast(frame, 1). The second call writes the frame's f_locals snapshot back into its cells (bpo-30744). _hook is a Python function, so while a section is open every event on that thread does this. The GIL can switch while _hook runs, so a closure (nonlocal) write made by another thread in that window is overwritten with the stale snapshot. The snapshot also keeps deleted locals alive until the frame's next own event, which changes refcount-driven behaviour. 3.11+ only write back when f_locals was materialised, and _hook never reads f_locals, so they are unaffected. Two ordinary harness shapes break only inside a section. (1) f09: a worker thread counts into a nonlocal while the section thread polls: 37k–136k of 300k updates are lost. A worker that sets `done = True` once has the flag reverted in 231–239 of 300 trials, so without the script's deadline the harness spins forever. (2) f09b, single-threaded and deterministic: `f = open(p,'w'); f.write('payload'); del f; read_back(p)` reads '' inside a section and 'payload' outside it. Untraced runs of both are clean. A related symptom: finalizers released by the trampoline run inside the profile callback, so on 3.10 their calls are invisible (probe_wr4.py), whereas L-RUNTIME says they count for the stack they land on.
